questions.worked_solution:
Remember that $cot$ is the reciprocal of $tan.$ So first we need to compute tangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{PR}{QR}=\frac{3}{QR}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the length $QR,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}-P{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3\sqrt{5})^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{45-9} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{-1}=2.
$$

So we have

Example: 
                    Evaluating Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratios Given a Triangle
canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\csc\theta,$ $\sec\theta,$ and $\cot\theta$ for the triangle below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224584/assets/343917ea041d51cac38619f3577765eee7fbc3ea85e175148b6c591e11ae230b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We compute the three reciprocal trigonometric ratios as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\csc\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac 5 3, \[5pt]
		\sec\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} =  \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac 5 4, \[5pt]
		\cot\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac 4 3.
	}
$$

Example: 
                    Evaluating a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio Given a Triangle Using the Pythagorean Theorem
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that $\sec$ is the reciprocal of $\cos.$ So first we need to compute cosine:

$$
\cos L = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JL}{KL} = \dfrac{JL}{5}
$$

To find the length $JL,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JL & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{K}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25-9} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\cos L = \dfrac{JL}{5} = \dfrac{4}{5},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡L & ={(\frac{4}{5})}^{-1}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The reciprocals of sine, cosine, and tangent are given special names:

- The reciprocal of **sine** is **cosecant**, abbreviated $\csc.$

$$
\csc(\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\sin(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}}
$$

- The reciprocal of **cosine** is **secant**, abbreviated $\sec.$

$$
\sec (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\cos(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}}
$$

- The reciprocal of **tangent** is **cotangent**, abbreviated $\cot.$

$$
\cot (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\tan(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{adjacent}}} = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}}
$$

Let's write down expressions for $\csc(B),$ $\sec(B),$ and $\cot(B)$ for the triangle below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224584/assets/e98dcc332739ff381e8dc43160a907e471062c5b8a75567ba7dbb8687c008efa.png)

$$
\eqalign{
		\csc(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac c b \[5pt]
		\sec(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac c a \[5pt]
		\cot(B) &= \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac a b \
	}
$$

tutorials.name: The Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratios and the Pythagorean Theorem
tutorials.problem:
If we are given two sides of a right triangle, how can we calculate the reciprocal ratios $\sec,$ $\csc,$ or $\cot$ when we are missing one of the necessary sides in the ratio?

The trick here is the same that we use for finding $\sin,$ $\cos,$ or $\tan\mathbin{:}$ we use the Pythagorean theorem for finding the missing side.

To illustrate, let's calculate $\csc L$  in the triangle below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224584/assets/9f2e4ea4922783c84a6cb59c5e1532b726d46c9a837a5b1eaa203bbdc6cc1741.png)

Remember that $\csc$ is the reciprocal of $\sin.$ So first we need to compute sine:

$$
\sin L = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JK}{KL} = \dfrac{JK}{4}
$$

To find the length $JK,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JK & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{L}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16-9} \\  & =\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\sin L = \dfrac{JK}{4} = \dfrac{ \sqrt{7} }{4},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡L & ={(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot \sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7}\cdot \sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$
